<!-- 1 ── RESULT IN ONE LINE -->
::: {.result-banner}
Cut voluntary churn 18% by targeting only the users a save-offer could actually persuade — worth ~$2.4M in retained ARR.
:::

<!-- 2 ── PROBLEM -->
## The problem

Retention was blanket-emailing every at-risk account a 20% discount, which was expensive and, for many users, unnecessary. The business needed to know *who* to spend the offer on, not just who was likely to leave. That distinction matters because the highest-churn-risk group mixes people who will leave regardless with people who'd have stayed anyway — spending on either is wasted.

<!-- 3 ── HERO CHART -->
## The finding

::: {#cell-fig-hero .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# NOTE: synthetic stand-in for the real holdout evaluation output.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
deciles = np.arange(1, 11)
uplift = np.array([9.5, 7.8, 5.9, 3.6, 1.9, 0.7, 0.1, -0.4, -1.1, -1.8]) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 10)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
colors = ["#2563eb" if u > 0 else "#c0c4cc" for u in uplift]
ax.bar(deciles, uplift, color=colors)
ax.axhline(0, color="#1f2328", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted-uplift decile (10 = most persuadable)")
ax.set_ylabel("Retention lift (pp)")
ax.set_xticks(deciles)
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color("#d5d5df"); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#d5d5df")
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#eef0f4", lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")  # thumbnail for /projects grid
plt.show()
```

Targeting the blue deciles and skipping the grey ones is the whole result: same budget, better spent.

<!-- 4 ── DECISIONS & TRADEOFFS (incl. failure) -->
## Decisions and tradeoffs

I framed this as uplift (treatment-effect) modeling rather than churn prediction — deliberate, because a well-calibrated churn model still can't tell you whether the offer *changed* anyone's behavior. I used a two-model T-learner over gradient-boosted trees and evaluated with the Qini coefficient on a held-out randomized slice. Keeping a genuine randomized holdout cost us offers we "knew" were good, but without it there's no honest way to measure uplift at all.

The first approach failed. A single S-learner with treatment as a feature collapsed the uplift signal — the treatment term was swamped by much stronger churn features, and predicted uplift came out nearly flat across deciles. Splitting into separate treatment and control models recovered it. I also tried a causal forest, which matched the T-learner on Qini but retrained slower and was harder to explain to the retention team, so I shipped the simpler model.

<!-- 5 ── MEASUREMENT + LIMITATIONS -->
## Measurement and limitations

Measured on the randomized holdout: retention lift by uplift decile (above) and the Qini coefficient — 0.21 versus 0.0 for random targeting. Two honest limitations. The model is trained on one offer (20% discount), so its uplift estimates won't transfer to a different intervention without re-randomizing. And the top decile is thin, so its point estimate carries a wide confidence interval. I'd re-run the holdout quarterly to catch drift as the user mix shifts.

<!-- 6 ── CODE, FOLDED -->
## How it works

::: {#6d4f3ada .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the T-learner + Qini evaluation"}
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

def fit_t_learner(X, y, treated):
    """Two-model uplift: P(retain | treated) - P(retain | control)."""
    m_t = HistGradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X[treated],  y[treated])
    m_c = HistGradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X[~treated], y[~treated])
    return m_t, m_c

def predict_uplift(m_t, m_c, X):
    return m_t.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] - m_c.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
```
:::
